prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and its first experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I opened with twisted bilayer graphene (B033) first and topological insulators (B009) second, and after reading the ballots I am moving B009 to the top of my configuration. It is the only shortlisted entry that seven of eight members placed in their top three, and the support comes from members with very different fields (condensed matter, atomic physics, statistical theory, astroparticle). That breadth is not equivalent to merit, but the scientific case stands independently: Kane and Mele identified a Z2 invariant that classifies band structures by topology, Molenkamp's group observed the predicted protected edge transport in HgTe wells, and about two decades of independent transport, ARPES and STM work have confirmed the picture across many materials. It is a discovery in the sense I stressed in my March 2026 lecture (as reported by Tohoku, a summary and not a transcript), not an accumulation of improvements, and the original work can be tied to named people through a clean theory-plus-experiment pairing. The 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and topological phases in low-dimensional models, not band topology of real insulators with protected edge states, so this is a distinct step.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp's group to look in HgTe is not among the credited names, and Hasan's observation of three-dimensional topological insulators is arguably as important as Mele's share in establishing the field as a materials class. Any trio therefore draws a line through a story that is spread across more than three people, and a Nobel-style prize risks leaving out contributors the community regards as essential. A second concern is that, after 2016, some will view this as a follow-on to the topological prize, and the direct technological payoff remains limited.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B009 first and regards the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio as natural but concedes that the credit between Hasan and Mele is genuinely contestable.
responses.response: I agree the contest is real, but I would keep Mele. The Kane-Mele Z2 paper and the graphene quantum spin Hall proposal came first and define the invariant that Hasan's 3D work then used, so the original idea is theirs. Hasan's ARPES observation is a major experimental result, but replacing Mele with him would leave the prediction half of the prize with one name and weaken the clean theory-experiment logic. I think the committee has to be explicit that the 3D experimental step and BHZ are acknowledged in the text but not credited.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B045 (tunnel magnetoresistance) second and proposed Miyazaki, Moodera and Parkin, noting the allocation problem between the 1995 room-temperature discovery and the MgO engineering step.
responses.response: I rated B045 highly because crystalline MgO barriers are a case where interface structure decides the physics, and I see it as both a discovery and an invention. But your own attribution argument is what holds me back: the 1995 discovery and the 2004 MgO step are two stages, the theory of coherent tunnelling by Butler and by Mathon and Umerski is outside the names, and any three people from the four credited ones either omit Miyazaki or omit Yuasa. That is a serious fairness problem which does not afflict B009 to the same degree. I would keep B045 as an alternative and not the lead, with the further caveat that it comes after the 2007 GMR prize.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B026 (optical lattice clocks) first and described it as the clearest case of a measurement discovery, while calling B009 a distinct and mature follow-on to 2016 that some may view as incremental.
responses.response: I do not see B009 as incremental. The 2016 prize recognized topological phase transitions and phases in model systems, whereas this work established that ordinary band structure carries a topological invariant with protected edge states, and then showed it in real crystals. I agree B026 has the cleanest two-person attribution on the list, and its maturity is not in doubt. My hesitation is that its overlap with the frequency-comb prize in 2005 and with ion-clock recognition may make it look more like refinement of precision than a new discovery. I would not oppose it as a laureate configuration, but I rank B009 higher on originality.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube (B024) first and argued that the instrument and the discovery of astrophysical neutrinos are of the first rank, while admitting the credit rests on a very large collaboration and the list supplies only Halzen.
responses.response: I accept that high-energy neutrino astronomy is a genuine discovery in nature. My concern is the one you raise yourself: a single credited name for a collaboration of hundreds is thin against the criterion of identifying the people responsible for the original work. If the committee wanted to proceed, I would want to know who conceived the detector and the analysis that found the flux before I could support Halzen alone, and as a non-specialist in this area I cannot settle that from the ballots. For now I do not see it as a stronger case than B009.

uncertainties: Whether Mele or Hasan should take the third slot, and how the committee should handle the absence of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from the credited names.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene (B033) is mature enough: the pairing mechanism is still debated and I rely on my own recollection of the chronology, including Andrei's early STM evidence.
Whether the committee would prefer a two-part prize pairing B009 with a second achievement, which the three-person limit would make hard to fit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B009 or for the alternatives named. My connections (Chalmers colleagues, David Clarke at IBM, Japanese academic exchanges) are not tied to any credited name on this shortlist, but I note that Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson works in the circuit QED field that bears on B010, which I have not proposed.
